relationship: historical connection through Anathoth
rationale: Jeremiah is introduced as a priest living in Anathoth. The later passage names men of Anathoth who demand that the prophet stop speaking in the Lord's name, connecting his hometown with opposition to his commission.

relationship: regnal chronology of Josiah's reforms and Jeremiah's calling
rationale: Jeremiah dates the beginning of God's word to Josiah's thirteenth year. Chronicles dates Josiah's beginning to cleanse Judah and Jerusalem to his twelfth year, providing adjacent regnal chronology without identifying the calling and the purge as the same event.

relationship: historical counterpart to Jerusalem's captivity
rationale: Jeremiah's heading ends with Zedekiah's eleventh year and Jerusalem's captivity in the fifth month. Kings records the siege lasting to Sedekias's eleventh year and the fifth-month destruction and removal of Jerusalem's population; the royal name forms differ.

relationship: parallel formation associated with the womb and commission toward nations
rationale: Jeremiah is known and consecrated before birth and appointed a prophet to nations. Isaiah describes one formed from the belly as God's servant and appointed a light for nations, sharing vocation associated with formation and an international scope without identifying the two speakers.

relationship: parallel objection about inability to speak when called
rationale: Jeremiah protests that he does not know how to speak because he is young. Moses similarly pleads weakness of voice and slowness of tongue; the grounds differ, but both objections arise when God commissions a speaker.

relationship: parallel prophetic obligation to speak God's commands
rationale: God tells Jeremiah to go to those to whom he is sent and speak everything commanded. Deuteronomy describes a prophet into whose mouth God puts His word and who speaks all God commands; this compares the commission rather than asserting an exclusive identification.

relationship: parallel assurance of divine presence against fear
rationale: Jeremiah receives the command not to fear because God is with him to rescue him. The Lord likewise tells Paul not to fear or cease speaking because He is with him, applying the assurance to a different threatened ministry.

relationship: shared image of God placing words in a mouth
rationale: The Lord touches Jeremiah's mouth and declares that He has put His words there. Isaiah also promises to put divine words in the addressee's mouth; the touching action belongs specifically to Jeremiah's account.

relationship: parallel authority to announce destruction and restoration of nations
rationale: The commission names uprooting, demolition, destruction, building and planting over nations and kingdoms. Jeremiah 18 explains God's speech about destroying a nation or kingdom and rebuilding and planting it, adding the conditions of repentance and disobedience.

relationship: parallel certainty that God's spoken word will be performed
rationale: God says He watches over His words to perform them. Isaiah compares the effective divine word to rain that produces growth and says it will not return before God's will is accomplished; it supports the performance promise without explaining the nut-wood vision.

relationship: parallel cauldron imagery in judgment upon Jerusalem
rationale: Jeremiah sees a cauldron heated from beneath, interpreted in the following verses through northern calamity. Ezekiel's cauldron parable explicitly addresses the city of bloodshed; both employ a heated cooking vessel for judgment, while Ezekiel's contents and rust are distinct details.

relationship: parallel announcement of northern calamity
rationale: The explanation of Jeremiah's vision says calamities will be kindled from the north upon the land's inhabitants. Jeremiah 6 again announces evils looking out from the north and great crushing, repeating the direction and destructive threat.

relationship: parallel gathering of northern forces against Zion
rationale: God summons northern kingdoms to set their thrones against Jerusalem's gates, walls and Judah's cities. Jeremiah 6 describes northern peoples and nations armed and drawn up for war against Zion, giving a corresponding military description without reproducing the thrones detail.

relationship: parallel condemnation of worshiping handmade objects
rationale: Jeremiah explains judgment by abandonment of God, sacrifice to foreign gods and bowing to human handiwork. Isaiah likewise condemns a land filled with abominations whose people bow before what their fingers made.

relationship: parallel fearless delivery of God's words despite hostile hearers
rationale: Jeremiah must rise, speak everything commanded and not fear his opponents. Ezekiel similarly receives the command not to fear hostile faces or words and to deliver God's words to the embittering house.

relationship: parallel strengthening of a prophet against opposition
rationale: Jeremiah is made like a fortified city and bronze wall against Judah's authorities and people. Ezekiel's face and contention are strengthened beyond rock against opponents; the comparison concerns divinely strengthened resistance, not identical material imagery.

relationship: repeated promise that opponents will not prevail against the prophet
rationale: The Lord promises that those fighting Jeremiah will not prevail because He is present to rescue him. Jeremiah 15 repeats the fight, failure to prevail and saving presence, then specifies rescue from evil and pestilent people.

relationship: parallel recollection of Israel's early relationship with God
rationale: Jeremiah recalls the mercy of Israel's youth and the love of its completion. Hosea likewise looks back to Israel's infancy and God's love before describing departure and Baal worship; Jeremiah's supplied wording is not replaced with a marriage-in-the-wilderness formulation.

relationship: parallel designation of Israel as holy to God
rationale: Jeremiah calls Israel holy to the Lord. Exodus describes covenant-keeping Israel as God's treasured people and a holy nation, providing a covenant counterpart to that sacred status.

relationship: shared firstfruits imagery for people belonging to God
rationale: Jeremiah calls Israel the first of the Lord's produce. James calls those born through the word of truth a kind of firstfruits of God's creatures; the shared agricultural imagery is clear, while the target does not repeat Jeremiah's warning against devouring Israel.

relationship: parallel futility resulting from departure into false worship
rationale: Israel's fathers followed futile things and became futile. Romans similarly describes people who fail to glorify God, become futile in thought and exchange divine glory for images, connecting distorted worship with the worshipers' own futility.

relationship: parallel remembrance of deliverance and guidance through a waterless wilderness
rationale: Jeremiah indicts those who fail to ask after the God who brought them from Egypt through an impassable, waterless wilderness. Deuteronomy warns against forgetting that same deliverance and guidance through a fearful wilderness where there was no water.

relationship: parallel defilement of the land by Israel's conduct
rationale: Jeremiah contrasts God's gift of fruitful land with the people's pollution of His inheritance. Ezekiel likewise says Israel defiled its land through its way, idols and uncleannesses and describes the resulting judgment and dispersal.

relationship: parallel indictment of corrupt civil and religious leadership
rationale: Jeremiah indicts several leadership groups, including law handlers who do not know God and prophets who speak by Baal. Micah similarly indicts leaders, priests and prophets, specifying distorted justice and paid religious service rather than Jeremiah's particular Baal charge.

relationship: related intergenerational judgment in a context of idolatry
rationale: Jeremiah announces judgment with the present people and their children's children after describing false worship. Exodus warns that the jealous God repays the sins of fathers upon later generations among those who hate Him; the connection does not assert that descendants are judged independently of their own conduct.

relationship: parallel exchange of glory for futile worship
rationale: Jeremiah says God's people exchanged their glory and will derive no benefit. The psalm specifies the exchange of their glory for the likeness of a grass-eating calf and the forgetting of their saving God.

relationship: related heavenly witness to Israel's rejection of God
rationale: Jeremiah portrays heaven as astonished and shuddering at the people's exchange. Isaiah summons heaven and earth to hear the Lord's charge that His children rejected and abandoned Him; the cosmic response differs from the summons to witness.

relationship: repeated description of abandoning the divine fountain of life
rationale: Jeremiah 2 names the Lord as a spring of water of life abandoned for broken cisterns. Jeremiah 17 again charges people with abandoning the Lord, the fountain of life, and attaches shame to that departure.

relationship: related living-water imagery with a contrasting human water source
rationale: Jeremiah contrasts the abandoned divine spring with cisterns unable to hold water. Jesus contrasts ordinary well water with His gift of living water becoming a spring toward eternal life; the target develops the water imagery without reproducing the accusation or broken cisterns.

relationship: contrast between Israel as God's son and Israel reduced to spoil
rationale: Jeremiah questions whether Israel is a slave or house-born servant in view of his becoming spoil. Exodus identifies Israel as God's firstborn son and demands his release for divine service, supplying a contrasting account of Israel's identity rather than a direct explanation of this later calamity.

relationship: parallel lion imagery for devastating invasion
rationale: Lions roar over Israel, making his land wilderness and cities uninhabited. Jeremiah 4 portrays a lion leaving its enclosure to destroy nations and make the land desolate and cities uninhabited, repeating the animal and the consequences.

relationship: parallel causal link between forsaking God and enemy domination
rationale: Jeremiah asks whether abandoning God brought the calamities upon the people. Judges explicitly joins Israel's forsaking the Lord and serving other gods with being delivered to plunderers and surrounding enemies.

relationship: parallel challenge to seeking security through Egypt
rationale: Jeremiah challenges the journey on Egypt's road to drink Gihon's water and also mentions the Assyrian road. Isaiah condemns going to Egypt for Pharaoh's help without consulting God; the shared Egyptward reliance does not require renaming Jeremiah's river.

relationship: parallel wrongdoing becoming the wrongdoer's own restraint or punishment
rationale: Jeremiah says apostasy will discipline the people and their evil will rebuke them. Proverbs says lawless deeds hunt a person and his own sins bind him, similarly depicting wrongdoing as returning upon its agent.

relationship: cultic counterpart to worship on hills and under trees
rationale: Jeremiah describes prostitution upon every high hill and beneath every shady tree after breaking bonds. Deuteronomy commands the destruction of foreign worship places on mountains, hills and under leafy trees, identifying the repeated locations as cultic settings.

relationship: parallel failure of a carefully planted divine vine
rationale: God planted a fruitful, genuine vine that became bitter and foreign. Isaiah's vineyard likewise receives careful planting but produces thorns instead of expected grapes; the images express failed cultivation while preserving each text's different bad outcome.

relationship: related washing imagery that cannot establish cleanness before God
rationale: Jeremiah says natron and cleansing herb cannot remove the stain of injustice before God. Job imagines washing with snow and clean hands yet being dipped in filth by God; his complaint and Jeremiah's accusation differ, but both deny that the imagined washing secures cleanness.

relationship: parallel pursuit of other lovers despite warning or obstruction
rationale: Jeremiah's woman answers the warning about her road and thirst with I will be strong, and the text says she loved strangers and followed them. Hosea's mother likewise declares that she will follow lovers, whose pursuit is then obstructed; the eventual return in Hosea is not asserted of Jeremiah's speaker.

relationship: parallel exposure of religious claims made toward manufactured objects
rationale: Jeremiah describes wood called a father and stone credited with birth, while people turn their backs on God. Isaiah describes a wooden remainder made into a god and addressed in prayer; this comparison concerns manufactured objects and avoids assigning Jeremiah's later cry for rescue specifically to the wood or stone.

relationship: parallel challenge that false gods should rise and rescue their worshipers
rationale: Jeremiah asks where Judah's manufactured gods are and whether they can rise and save in affliction. Deuteronomy similarly asks where the trusted gods are, challenges them to rise and help, and contrasts them with God's unrivaled power.

relationship: parallel failure to respond to repeated divine discipline
rationale: Jeremiah says blows upon the children were vain because discipline was not accepted. Amos repeatedly recounts blows, sword and destruction followed by failure to turn to God, matching the indictment of unresponsive recipients without equating every punishment.

relationship: related indictment of rejecting the God who sustained Israel
rationale: God asks whether He became a wilderness or barren land to Israel while the people reject His rule. Deuteronomy describes the nourished and satisfied people forsaking their Maker and forgetting the God who nourishes them, supplying the corresponding contrast between divine provision and rejection.

relationship: contrast between the people's forgetfulness and God's refusal to forget
rationale: Jeremiah compares the people's long forgetfulness of God with the implausibility of a bride or virgin forgetting adornment. Isaiah answers Zion's complaint of being forgotten with God's refusal to forget her; the direction of the forgetting is reversed.

relationship: legal contrast distinguishing innocent blood from a fatal break-in
rationale: Jeremiah charges bloodshed against innocent lives and explicitly says they were not found in break-ins. Exodus excludes murder in the death of a thief found breaking in and then distinguishes a case after sunrise; this supplies a legal contrast without resolving the target's later pronouns or Jeremiah's oak detail.

relationship: parallel rejection of a claim to have no sin
rationale: Jeremiah announces judgment precisely because the people say they did not sin. First John likewise rejects claims of having no sin or not having sinned and contrasts them with confession and cleansing.

relationship: parallel shame resulting from reliance on Egypt
rationale: Jeremiah predicts that Egypt will put the people to shame as Assyria did. Isaiah likewise says Pharaoh's shelter and the hoped-for Egyptian assistance will become shame and reproach rather than benefit.

relationship: shared gesture of departing with hands on the head
rationale: Jeremiah predicts departure with hands upon the head after the Lord rejects the people's hope. Tamar likewise leaves with her hands on her head and cries out; the visible gesture is shared, while her victimization must not be treated as the same moral situation as Judah's judgment.

relationship: legal background to the divorce and remarriage question
rationale: Jeremiah asks whether a dismissed wife who becomes another man's will return to her former husband, before confronting the people's many shepherds. Deuteronomy forbids the former husband from taking such a wife back after the intervening marriage, supplying the stated legal analogy rather than resolving all the prophetic question's implications.

relationship: parallel roadside prostitution imagery for covenant infidelity
rationale: Jeremiah portrays the woman seated on roads and polluting the land through prostitution. Ezekiel's address to Jerusalem describes prostitution chambers in broad streets and at road heads, giving a particular counterpart to the public locations without reproducing the solitary-crow image.

relationship: parallel prostitute appearance and shameless face
rationale: Jeremiah charges the people with a prostitute's appearance and shamelessness. Proverbs describes the seductress with a prostitute's appearance and a shameless face; Jeremiah applies such language collectively rather than narrating the same individual encounter.

relationship: related appeal to divine fatherhood amid covenant infidelity
rationale: Jeremiah recalls calling God a father and leader of virginity amid accusations of faithlessness. Malachi asks whether all have one Father and then indicts covenant profanation and devotion to foreign gods, likewise exposing a gap between the paternal relationship and conduct.

relationship: parallel prostitution imagery linked with hilltop and tree-shaded worship
rationale: Jeremiah describes Israel's prostitution on high mountains and beneath wooded trees. Hosea similarly joins a spirit of prostitution and departure from God with sacrifices on mountaintops, hills and beneath named shade trees.

relationship: parallel divine summons met by departure rather than return
rationale: God calls Israel to return, but she does not. Hosea likewise recalls God's summons followed by departure from His presence and sacrifice to Baalim; Jeremiah additionally says Judah observed Israel's faithlessness.

relationship: related divorce-document imagery for separation caused by unfaithfulness
rationale: Jeremiah explicitly says God sent Israel away and gave her a divorce certificate. Isaiah asks about the mother's divorce document and attributes her dismissal to lawless acts; the rhetorical question and Jeremiah's explicit giving of a document are kept distinct.

relationship: parallel association of adultery imagery with idolatry
rationale: Jeremiah describes adultery with wood and stone. Ezekiel combines adultery with reflections, child offerings and the explicit mention of idols, placing false worship within the same language of marital unfaithfulness without replacing the target's unusual wording.

relationship: parallel contrast between outward religious approach and a distant heart
rationale: Judah's return is described as false rather than wholehearted. Isaiah similarly contrasts honoring God with lips and a heart far from Him, providing a precise counterpart to outward response lacking inward fidelity.

relationship: parallel relative justification through another community's greater wrongdoing
rationale: Jeremiah says Israel is justified in comparison with faithless Judah. Ezekiel says Jerusalem's greater lawlessness justified her sisters, including Samaria; neither comparison declares the less guilty community absolutely innocent.

relationship: parallel divine mercy and anger that does not last forever
rationale: God invites Israel to return because He is merciful and will not remain angry forever. The psalm likewise calls Him compassionate and merciful and says He does not maintain wrath forever.

relationship: parallel acknowledgment of wrongdoing as the proper response
rationale: Jeremiah demands recognition of injustice, disobedience and departure toward strangers. First John describes confession of sins together with divine forgiveness and cleansing; the shared response is acknowledgment rather than a denial of wrongdoing.

relationship: parallel gathering of a scattered remnant
rationale: God promises to take small numbers from cities and clans and bring them to Zion. Isaiah likewise promises recovery of a remaining remnant and the gathering of Israel's lost and Judah's scattered people, with a wider geographical enumeration rather than Jeremiah's numerical expressions.

relationship: parallel divine provision of shepherds for the restored people
rationale: Jeremiah promises shepherds according to God's heart who shepherd with knowledge. Ezekiel promises one shepherd, God's servant David, over the people; the divine provision is common, while the plural shepherds and the single named shepherd are distinct.

relationship: parallel future gathering of nations to Jerusalem
rationale: Jeremiah says Jerusalem will be called the Lord's throne and nations will gather there. Isaiah likewise describes nations coming to the Lord's mountain and receiving His way, with law and the Lord's word proceeding from Zion and Jerusalem.

relationship: parallel reunion of divided Israel in the inherited land
rationale: Jeremiah promises that Judah will join Israel and return together from northern and other regions. Ezekiel promises gathering into Israel's land and an end to division into two nations or kingdoms, giving a corresponding account of reunion.

relationship: parallel acknowledgment of God as Father in relation to inheritance
rationale: Jeremiah anticipates the people calling God Father and receiving a chosen inheritance. Isaiah's prayer calls the Lord Father and appeals concerning the tribes of His inheritance and the holy mountain; its petition differs from Jeremiah's promise.

relationship: parallel portrayal of the people's infidelity through a broken marriage
rationale: Jeremiah compares Israel's faithlessness with a woman's faithlessness toward her partner. Hosea likewise portrays the mother through prostitution and the repudiated wife-husband relationship, using marital language for the people's departure.

relationship: parallel weeping associated with returning from wrongdoing
rationale: Jeremiah hears the weeping and supplication of Israel's children after their unjust ways and forgetting God. Joel calls for return to God with weeping, mourning and a torn heart, giving the corresponding summons to penitential sorrow.

relationship: parallel summons to return followed by a promise of healing
rationale: Jeremiah calls the returning children back and promises to heal their fractures. Hosea calls Israel to return with words and later promises to heal their dwellings; the return-and-healing pattern is shared while fractures and dwellings remain different expressions.

relationship: related contrast between looking toward mountains and finding help in God
rationale: Jeremiah declares the hills and the mountains' power false and locates Israel's salvation in the Lord. The psalm looks toward the mountains, asks where help comes from and answers that it comes from the Lord; it does not itself call the mountains false.

relationship: parallel loss of livestock, children and the fruit of labor
rationale: Jeremiah says shame consumed the fathers' labors, sheep, calves, sons and daughters. Deuteronomy's curse similarly describes livestock and children given away and an unknown nation consuming the people's labor; it supplies a concrete loss pattern without identifying Jeremiah's personified shame as that nation.

relationship: parallel corporate confession of longstanding sin and shame
rationale: Jeremiah's speakers lie in shame and confess that they and their fathers sinned from youth to the present. Ezra likewise confesses accumulated lawlessness from the fathers' days to the present and speaks of shame before God.

relationship: parallel summons to return and renounce false worship
rationale: Jeremiah conditions Israel's return on removing abominations from the mouth and reverence before God. Hosea similarly calls Israel to return with words and renounce calling human handiwork gods, joining verbal response with rejection of false worship.

relationship: parallel demand for truth, just judgment and truthful oaths
rationale: Jeremiah describes swearing that the Lord lives with truth, judgment and righteousness. Zechariah likewise commands truth and peaceful judgment while rejecting love of a false oath; Jeremiah additionally anticipates blessing among nations.

relationship: related cultivation imagery for a righteous response to God
rationale: Jeremiah commands breaking fallow ground and avoiding sowing among thorns. Hosea commands sowing in righteousness, reaping life's fruit and seeking the Lord; its supplied wording does not repeat the fallow-ground command, but both frame the needed response through cultivation.

relationship: repeated command to circumcise hardness of heart
rationale: Jeremiah calls Judah and Jerusalem to circumcise their hardness of heart. Deuteronomy gives the same inward command and adds that they must no longer stiffen their neck, clarifying the obedience sought through the image.

relationship: related interpretation of circumcision as an inward matter
rationale: Jeremiah directs circumcision toward hardness of heart rather than merely a physical act. Romans likewise speaks of circumcision of the heart in Spirit and inward identity; its argument about who is a Jew is not explicitly stated in Jeremiah's warning.

relationship: parallel trumpet alarm addressed to Zion's region
rationale: Jeremiah commands a trumpet signal and loud warning in Judah and Jerusalem as people gather toward walled cities. Joel similarly commands the trumpet in Zion and proclamation on the holy mountain, explaining the alarm through the announced Lord's day.

relationship: repeated warning of northern evils and great crushing
rationale: Jeremiah urges flight to Zion because evils and great crushing are coming from the north. Jeremiah 6 repeats the northern direction and great crushing while addressing Benjamin and calling for warning signals.

relationship: parallel lion imagery producing desolated land and empty cities
rationale: The departing lion destroys nations and leaves the land desolate and cities without inhabitants. Jeremiah 2 likewise joins roaring lions with wilderness and demolished, uninhabited cities, giving a close earlier form of the same destructive imagery.

relationship: parallel summons to sackcloth and lament under divine calamity
rationale: Jeremiah commands sackcloth, mourning and wailing because the Lord's fury has not turned away. Joel likewise summons ministers to lament and sleep in sackcloth, then announces the near day of the Lord; the addressees and immediate reasons differ.

relationship: parallel collapse of civil and religious leadership during judgment
rationale: Jeremiah describes the failure of kings and rulers and the astonishment of priests and prophets. Ezekiel likewise depicts the loss of priestly law and elders' counsel, a sought prophetic vision and a ruler clothed in devastation, showing institutions overwhelmed by judgment.

relationship: parallel exposure of proclaimed peace contradicted by reality
rationale: Jeremiah protests that a promise of peace is contradicted by a sword reaching the people's soul. Jeremiah 6 likewise exposes the claim of peace by asking where peace is; that later charge against those treating the fracture does not settle every question about Jeremiah's address to God here.

relationship: parallel rapid invading cavalry compared with an eagle
rationale: Jeremiah describes stormlike chariots and horses swifter than eagles. Habakkuk's Chaldean warriors likewise rush from afar with horsemen flying like an eagle, using the bird's speed to depict invasion while retaining distinct animal comparisons.

relationship: parallel command to wash away moral evil
rationale: Jeremiah orders Jerusalem to wash its heart of evil rather than retain harmful schemes. Isaiah likewise commands washing, removal of evils from souls and cessation of evil deeds, making the cleansing explicitly moral.

relationship: repeated northern warning associated with Dan
rationale: Jeremiah anticipates an announcing voice from Dan and trouble from Ephraim. Jeremiah 8 again locates an alarming sound at Dan, this time the horses of an approaching destroyer; the source's announcement and the target's cavalry sound remain distinct.

relationship: parallel threat from distant forces
rationale: Jeremiah announces bands from a distant land raising their voice against Judah's cities. Isaiah likewise describes a signal among distant nations and their rapid, armed arrival, giving the military counterpart to the distant bands.

relationship: parallel encirclement of Jerusalem
rationale: Jeremiah compares the forces around the city to those guarding a field. Jeremiah 6 depicts shepherds and flocks pitching tents against Zion all around, repeating the surrounding position through a different rural image.

relationship: repeated explanation that the people's own evil brings bitter consequences
rationale: Jeremiah attributes what happened to the people's ways and practices and calls the result bitter. Jeremiah 2 similarly says apostasy and evil will discipline and rebuke them and describes abandonment of God as bitter.

relationship: parallel bodily pain and a troubled heart amid an ominous message
rationale: Jeremiah speaks of pain in the belly, a torn heart and the heard cry of war. Isaiah's speaker likewise describes a harsh vision, bodily weakness, labor pains and a wandering, fearful heart; the particular vision and Jeremiah's trumpet report are distinct.

relationship: repeated lament over a ruined tent and torn coverings
rationale: Jeremiah laments sudden misery affecting the tent and torn coverings. Jeremiah 10 again describes the tent's misery and destruction and all its coverings torn, then adds the loss of sons and sheep.

relationship: same-chapter recurrence of the trumpet heard in distress
rationale: The question about how long flight and trumpet sounds will continue resumes the earlier voice's distress at a trumpet and cry of war. The explicit repeated sound connects the lamenting question with the preceding bodily anguish.

relationship: contrast between skill in evil and wisdom in goodness
rationale: Jeremiah calls the leaders of the people wise at evil but untrained in doing good. Paul desires the opposite orientation: wisdom about good and innocence about evil, furnishing a sharply reversed moral pattern.

relationship: literary contrast with the appearance of earth and light in creation
rationale: Jeremiah looks at earth and sees nothing, and finds heaven's lights absent. Genesis moves from the unseen, unformed earth and darkness to God's creation of light; the comparison reads Jeremiah's desolation against creation without substituting Genesis's wording for Jeremiah's.

relationship: parallel trembling of mountains and hills before divine wrath
rationale: Jeremiah sees mountains trembling and hills shaken in a scene explained through the Lord's anger. Nahum likewise describes mountains and hills shaking before Him and asks who can resist His furious wrath.

relationship: contrast with creation's birds and humanity
rationale: Jeremiah's vision contains no human and birds of heaven in terror. Genesis describes the making and blessing of birds and the making of humanity; human absence and frightened birds invert the ordered, populated creation without saying Jeremiah's birds are absent.

relationship: parallel change of Carmel or Chermel into wilderness
rationale: Jeremiah sees Carmel become wilderness amid burned cities. Isaiah's supplied text likewise says Chermel will become wilderness after describing abandoned houses and a deserted city, providing the same direction of change with a different form of the place-name.

relationship: repeated limit on destruction: no complete end
rationale: Jeremiah announces wilderness for the land but expressly excludes a complete end. Jeremiah 5 repeats God's promise not to bring the people to a complete end amid the invasion warnings.

relationship: parallel declaration that God's announced purpose will not be reversed
rationale: Jeremiah explains mourning and darkened heaven by God's settled speech and refusal to turn back. Isaiah likewise says what God spoke and counseled will stand and asks who can turn back His hand, though that oracle specifically concerns Assyria.

relationship: parallel refuge in caves and rocks under overwhelming threat
rationale: Jeremiah describes flight into caves, groves and rocks at cavalry and bows. Isaiah likewise describes entry into rock clefts and holes before the Lord's terror; the refuges correspond while the stated immediate threats differ.

relationship: parallel painted eyes and ornaments within a condemned lovers image
rationale: Jeremiah describes scarlet, gold ornaments and eyes painted with antimony as futile because the lovers seek her life. Ezekiel similarly describes painted eyes, ornaments and approaching men within its adultery accusation; it subsequently announces punishment rather than repeating Jeremiah's exact rejection by lovers.

relationship: parallel portrayal of Zion's distress as childbirth
rationale: Jeremiah hears Zion groaning like a woman giving birth for the first time and failing over the killed. Micah likewise addresses Zion through labor pains and a woman giving birth, adding exile and promised rescue rather than Jeremiah's particular lament over deaths.

relationship: parallel mercy for a city conditional on finding righteous people
rationale: Jeremiah calls for a search for even one person doing justice and seeking faithfulness, with mercy promised if found. Genesis likewise presents sparing Sodom for righteous inhabitants, with the requested numbers descending to ten rather than Jeremiah's one.

relationship: contrast between truthful and false use of the same oath
rationale: Jeremiah 5 exposes falsehood beneath the oath that the Lord lives. Jeremiah 4 describes that same oath uttered with truth, judgment and righteousness, making the required quality of the oath explicit.

relationship: parallel resistance to correction despite repeated punishment
rationale: Jeremiah says the people refuse instruction and refuse to return even after scourging and devastation. Amos likewise recounts destructive blows and repeatedly says that the people still did not turn to God.

relationship: same-chapter contrast between poor and prosperous people in disobedience
rationale: The speaker first considers people who may be poor and lack ability and knowledge of God's way. He then proposes going to prosperous people who recognized that way and judgment, yet reports that they broke the yoke too; the shared failure cuts across the stated contrast in means and knowledge.

relationship: parallel defiance expressed as tearing bonds and rejecting a yoke
rationale: The prosperous people together break the yoke and tear bonds despite recognizing God's way. The psalm likewise portrays kings and rulers opposing the Lord and His anointed by proposing to tear bonds and cast off the yoke; the groups are not identical.

relationship: parallel predatory animals in the judgment of Israel
rationale: Jeremiah describes lion, wolf and leopard attacks because of multiplied impieties. Hosea likewise threatens Israel through panther, leopard, distressed bear and devouring forest lion cubs; the overlapping predators reinforce the judgment image without making the animal lists identical.

relationship: parallel abandonment of God after being filled by His provision
rationale: Jeremiah contrasts feeding the people fully with their abandonment, false oaths and adultery. Deuteronomy likewise describes Jacob eating and being filled before forsaking the nourishing God and turning to foreign gods.

relationship: commandment counterpart to desire for a neighbor's wife
rationale: Jeremiah compares the people's desire for their neighbors' wives to horses mad for mares. Exodus explicitly prohibits coveting a neighbor's wife, supplying the command violated by the depicted desire.

relationship: repeated refrain of visitation and vengeance for wrongdoing
rationale: Jeremiah asks whether God will not visit and take vengeance after the accusations of adultery. Jeremiah 9 repeats the same two questions after deceitful speech and concealed enmity, applying the recurring judgment refrain to another form of wrong.

relationship: parallel command or promise limiting total destruction
rationale: Jeremiah 5 commands the tearing down of battlements while forbidding a complete end and preserving supports belonging to the Lord. Jeremiah 4 similarly announces desolation while excluding a complete end; its general limit corresponds without turning the supports into vine branches.

relationship: parallel indictment of both Israel and Judah
rationale: Jeremiah 5 says both houses utterly rejected God. Jeremiah 3 separately describes Israel's adultery and dismissal and Judah's fearless imitation and false return, supplying the two-house pattern behind the collective charge.

relationship: parallel denial that calamity will reach God's people
rationale: Jeremiah reports the denial that evils, sword or famine will come. Amos likewise condemns sinners among God's people who say evils will not approach them and expressly announces death by sword.

relationship: parallel prophecy lacking divine authorization
rationale: Jeremiah calls the prophets wind and says the Lord's word was not in them. Ezekiel similarly condemns prophets speaking from their own hearts, seeing false things and claiming the Lord spoke although He did not send them.

relationship: repeated image of God's word as fire
rationale: God makes His words fire in Jeremiah's mouth and the people wood to be consumed. Jeremiah 23 again describes the divine words as blazing fire while contrasting them with false prophetic dreams; the wood metaphor is specific to Jeremiah 5.

relationship: parallel distant invading nation with unintelligible speech
rationale: Jeremiah announces a nation from far away whose language Israel will not understand. Deuteronomy's curse likewise brings a distant nation whose speech is not understood, adding its merciless character.

relationship: parallel consumption of produce and livestock and defeat of trusted fortifications
rationale: Jeremiah describes an invader consuming the harvest, animals and orchard produce and threshing fortified cities trusted by the people. Deuteronomy likewise describes cattle and produce consumed and the collapse of high fortified walls in which they trust.

relationship: parallel judgment that stops short of completely removing Israel
rationale: Jeremiah promises that the invasion will not bring the people to a complete end. Amos similarly announces removal of the sinful kingdom but expressly says Jacob's house will not be completely removed.

relationship: parallel transfer into enemy service after failure to serve God faithfully
rationale: Jeremiah explains foreign servitude by service to foreign gods in the people's own land. Deuteronomy likewise contrasts failure to serve the Lord properly with enforced service to enemies in deprivation, preserving the different descriptions of the original disobedience.

relationship: parallel unseeing eyes and unhearing ears among God's people
rationale: Jeremiah addresses a foolish people who have eyes but do not see and ears but do not hear. Isaiah's commission similarly describes hearing without understanding and seeing without perception, expanding the image through dull hearts and closed eyes.

relationship: parallel divine establishment of a boundary the sea cannot cross
rationale: Jeremiah names sand as the sea's boundary and says roaring waves cannot cross God's command. In Job, God likewise sets the sea's boundaries with bars and gates and tells its waves they may go no farther; the boundary's imagery differs.

relationship: parallel disobedient hearts and departure from God's direction
rationale: Jeremiah 5 says the people acquired an unheeding, disobedient heart and turned away. Jeremiah 7 likewise joins failure to hear with following the evil heart's thoughts, moving backward and hardening the neck.

relationship: parallel divine gift of seasonal early and late rains for harvest
rationale: Jeremiah indicts failure to fear the God who gives early and late rains and preserves the harvest's appointed fulfillment. Deuteronomy promises those seasonal rains and the gathering of grain, wine and oil in connection with faithful service.

relationship: parallel loss of agricultural good through disobedience
rationale: Jeremiah explains the loss of the preceding gifts through lawless acts and sins. Deuteronomy likewise warns that turning to other gods will lead to closed heaven, withheld rain and failed produce.

relationship: parallel wicked people laying traps for human victims
rationale: Jeremiah finds impious people setting traps to destroy and catch men. The psalm likewise asks rescue from unjust people who devise stumbling and hide traps and cords for the speaker's feet.

relationship: parallel enrichment of houses through predatory wrongdoing
